category: Descriptive statistics, data reduction, interpolation & polynomials
description: Reductions and cumulative operations over arrays, descriptive statistics and moving-window smoothing, missing-data and outlier handling, one- and multi-dimensional interpolation including gridded and scattered data, and the polynomial fitting, evaluation and calculus functions built into core MATLAB.

tools.name: sum
tools.description: Adds elements along a dimension, over all dimensions with 'all', or over a list of dimensions. Use it for totals, inner products, counting logical trues and marginalizing probability tables. The 'omitnan' flag skips missing values instead of propagating NaN.
tools.usage:
S = sum(A)
S = sum(A, dim)
S = sum(A, 'all')
S = sum(___, nanflag)
S = sum(___, outtype)

parameters.name: dim
parameters.description: Dimension or vector of dimensions to sum over.

parameters.name: outtype
parameters.description: 'default', 'double' or 'native' to control the accumulator class.

tools.example:
A = magic(4);
sum(A)
sum(A, 2)'
sum(A, 'all')
sum([1 NaN 3], 'omitnan')
sum(int8([100 100]), 'native')
tools.notes: Summing a single-precision or integer array in 'native' mode can saturate or lose precision; the default accumulates integers in their native class but singles in single. `sum(mask)` counts true elements of a logical array.

tools.name: prod
tools.description: Multiplies elements along a dimension or over the whole array. Use it for products of probabilities, for computing the number of elements from a size vector, and for cumulative growth factors. Products of many values overflow or underflow quickly, so work with logs when the factors are far from 1.
tools.usage:
B = prod(A)
B = prod(A, dim)
B = prod(A, 'all')
B = prod(___, nanflag)
tools.notes: For long products of probabilities, `exp(sum(log(p)))` avoids underflow. prod of an empty array is 1, the multiplicative identity.

tools.name: cumsum
tools.description: Returns the running total along a dimension, with the same size as the input. Use it for discrete integration of a sampled signal, for building cumulative distribution functions, and for prefix-sum algorithms that turn loops into vectorized code. Direction and NaN handling are both configurable.
tools.usage:
B = cumsum(A)
B = cumsum(A, dim)
B = cumsum(___, direction)
B = cumsum(___, nanflag)
tools.example:
cumsum([1 2 3 4])
cumsum([1 2 3 4], 'reverse')
counts = [3 1 4 1 5];
cdf = cumsum(counts) / sum(counts)
cumsum([1 NaN 3], 'omitnan')
tools.notes: Long cumulative sums accumulate rounding error; for high accuracy over millions of samples consider compensated summation or double precision. `cumtrapz` integrates with trapezoidal weighting instead.

tools.name: cumprod
tools.description: Returns the running product along a dimension. Use it for compound growth series, cumulative survival probabilities and factorial-like sequences. As with `prod`, values can overflow or underflow rapidly, so a log-domain cumulative sum is often the safer formulation.
tools.usage:
B = cumprod(A)
B = cumprod(A, dim)
B = cumprod(___, direction)
B = cumprod(___, nanflag)
tools.example:
cumprod([1 2 3 4])
returns = [0.02 -0.01 0.03];
growth = cumprod(1 + returns)
cumprod(1:20)
tools.notes: cumprod(1:171) overflows to Inf. Use `exp(cumsum(log(x)))` for positive x when the values span many orders of magnitude.

tools.name: diff
tools.description: Computes differences between adjacent elements, optionally applying the operation n times to approximate higher derivatives. The output is one element shorter along the operating dimension. Use it for numerical differentiation on a uniform grid, for detecting changes and steps, and for checking whether a vector is sorted.
tools.usage:
Y = diff(X)
Y = diff(X, n)
Y = diff(X, n, dim)

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Order of the difference; defaults to 1.

tools.notes: diff amplifies noise; for noisy data use `gradient`, which is centred and keeps the original length, or smooth first. Each extra order removes one more element.

tools.name: max
tools.description: Returns the largest elements along a dimension, elementwise maxima of two arrays, or the k largest values. The second output gives the index of the maximum, which is how you find where a peak occurs. NaN values are ignored by default.
tools.usage:
M = max(A)
[M, I] = max(A)
M = max(A, [], dim)
C = max(A, B)
[M, I] = max(A, [], 'all', 'linear')
B = maxk(A, k)

parameters.name: dim
parameters.description: Dimension to reduce along; pass [] as the second argument when using dim.

parameters.name: 'linear'
parameters.description: Return a linear index rather than a subscript.

tools.notes: `max(A, B)` compares two arrays elementwise while `max(A, [], dim)` reduces one array, so the empty second argument is required when specifying a dimension. Only the first occurrence index is returned for ties; use `find(v == max(v))` for all of them.

tools.name: min
tools.description: Returns the smallest elements along a dimension, elementwise minima of two arrays, or the k smallest values with `mink`. Like `max` it provides an index output and ignores NaN by default. Use it for clamping values, finding best-scoring candidates and computing ranges.
tools.usage:
M = min(A)
[M, I] = min(A)
M = min(A, [], dim)
C = min(A, B)
B = mink(A, k)
tools.notes: Clamping with `min(max(x,lo),hi)` is the standard idiom. `bounds(x)` returns the minimum and maximum in one call.

tools.name: bounds
tools.description: Returns the smallest and largest elements of an array in a single call, along a dimension or over all elements. Use it to compute data ranges for axis limits and normalization without calling min and max separately. NaN values are omitted by default.
tools.usage:
[S, L] = bounds(A)
[S, L] = bounds(A, dim)
[S, L] = bounds(A, 'all')
[S, L] = bounds(___, nanflag)
tools.notes: bounds traverses the data once instead of twice, which matters for very large arrays. For normalization, `normalize(A,'range')` does the whole job in one step.

tools.name: mean
tools.description: Computes the arithmetic mean along a dimension, over all elements with 'all', or over selected dimensions. Use it for averaging measurements, centring data and summarizing groups. The 'omitnan' flag ignores missing values, and an output type can force double accumulation for single or integer input.
tools.usage:
M = mean(A)
M = mean(A, dim)
M = mean(A, 'all')
M = mean(___, outtype)
M = mean(___, nanflag)
tools.notes: The mean of an integer array is returned as double by default. For a weighted mean use `sum(w.*x)/sum(w)`; core MATLAB has no weighted mean function.

tools.name: median
tools.description: Computes the median, the middle value of sorted data, which is robust to outliers unlike the mean. For an even number of elements it averages the two central values. Use it for skewed distributions, for robust centre estimates and as a baseline in outlier detection.
tools.usage:
M = median(A)
M = median(A, dim)
M = median(A, 'all')
M = median(___, nanflag)
tools.example:
median([1 2 3 100])
mean([1 2 3 100])
A = magic(4);
median(A, 2)'
median([1 NaN 3], 'omitnan')
tools.notes: median sorts internally, so it is O(n log n) rather than O(n). The median absolute deviation, `median(abs(x - median(x)))`, is the robust scale estimate used by `isoutlier`.

tools.name: mode
tools.description: Returns the most frequently occurring value, choosing the smallest when several values tie. Use it for categorical-like numeric data, for finding the dominant label in a neighbourhood, and for imputing discrete missing values. The second and third outputs give the frequency and all tied values.
tools.usage:
M = mode(A)
M = mode(A, dim)
[M, F, C] = mode(___)
tools.example:
[m, f, c] = mode([3 3 1 4 4])
mode([1 2 2 3 3])
labels = [1 1 2 2 2 3];
mode(labels)
tools.notes: mode ignores NaN. For continuous data the mode of the raw samples is meaningless; bin with `histcounts` first and take the peak bin.

tools.name: std
tools.description: Computes the standard deviation, normalizing by N-1 by default to give the unbiased sample estimate. Pass a weight flag of 1 for the population standard deviation, or a weight vector for a weighted estimate. Use it for measuring spread, error bars and signal-to-noise ratios.
tools.usage:
S = std(A)
S = std(A, w)
S = std(A, w, dim)
S = std(___, nanflag)

parameters.name: w
parameters.description: 0 for N-1 normalization (default), 1 for N, or a weight vector.

tools.example:
x = [2 4 4 4 5 5 7 9];
std(x)
std(x, 1)
std(x, 0, 2)
std([1 NaN 3], 'omitnan')
tools.notes: std(A) of a matrix gives one value per column. Standard error of the mean is `std(x)/sqrt(numel(x))`. `std` equals sqrt(var) with the same weight flag.

tools.name: var
tools.description: Computes the variance, the square of the standard deviation, with the same N-1 default normalization and weighting options as `std`. Use it in error propagation, analysis of variance and when comparing variability across groups. Working in variance rather than standard deviation avoids repeated square roots.
tools.usage:
V = var(A)
V = var(A, w)
V = var(A, w, dim)
V = var(___, nanflag)

parameters.name: w
parameters.description: 0 for N-1 (default), 1 for N, or a weight vector.

tools.notes: For a matrix, `var(A)` gives per-column variances while `cov(A)` gives the full covariance matrix whose diagonal equals those variances.

tools.name: cov
tools.description: Computes the covariance matrix of the columns of a matrix, or the 2-by-2 covariance of two vectors. Use it for principal component analysis, for error ellipses, and for characterizing correlated noise. The diagonal holds the variances of the individual variables.
tools.usage:
C = cov(A)
C = cov(A, B)
C = cov(___, w)
C = cov(___, nanflag)

parameters.name: A
parameters.description: Matrix whose columns are variables and rows are observations.

parameters.name: w
parameters.description: 0 for N-1 normalization (default) or 1 for N.

tools.notes: cov subtracts the column means first. The eigenvectors of the covariance matrix are the principal directions, which is PCA without a toolbox.

tools.name: corrcoef
tools.description: Computes the matrix of Pearson linear correlation coefficients between columns, scaled so that every value lies in [-1, 1]. Additional outputs give p-values and confidence bounds for the hypothesis of no correlation. Use it for quick dependency screening between variables.
tools.usage:
R = corrcoef(A)
R = corrcoef(x, y)
[R, P] = corrcoef(___)
[R, P, RL, RU] = corrcoef(___)
R = corrcoef(___, 'Rows', 'complete')

parameters.name: 'Rows'
parameters.description: 'all' (default), 'complete' to drop rows with NaN, or 'pairwise'.

parameters.name: 'Alpha'
parameters.description: Significance level for the confidence bounds; defaults to 0.05.

tools.notes: Pearson correlation only measures linear association and is sensitive to outliers. For rank correlation you need `corr` from Statistics and Machine Learning Toolbox.

tools.name: histcounts
tools.description: Bins data and returns the counts and bin edges without drawing anything, using an automatic binning algorithm by default. Use it to compute histograms for further processing, to build empirical distributions, and to discretize continuous data. Normalization options turn counts into probabilities or densities.
tools.usage:
[N, edges] = histcounts(X)
[N, edges] = histcounts(X, nbins)
[N, edges] = histcounts(X, edges)
[N, edges, bin] = histcounts(___)
N = histcounts(___, 'Normalization', method)

parameters.name: edges
parameters.description: Explicit bin edges; bins are left-closed except the last.

parameters.name: 'BinLimits'
parameters.description: Two-element vector limiting the range that is binned.

tools.notes: Bins are half-open [a,b) except the final bin which includes its right edge. `histcounts2` bins bivariate data and `discretize` returns only the bin index per observation.

tools.name: movmean
tools.description: Computes a moving average over a sliding window of fixed length or an asymmetric [before after] span. Use it to smooth noisy time series, to compute rolling baselines and to estimate slowly varying trends. Endpoint handling can shrink the window, discard incomplete windows or fill with a constant.
tools.usage:
M = movmean(A, k)
M = movmean(A, [kb kf])
M = movmean(___, dim)
M = movmean(___, 'Endpoints', ep)
M = movmean(___, 'SamplePoints', t)

parameters.name: k
parameters.description: Window length; centred when a scalar.

parameters.name: [kb kf]
parameters.description: Elements before and after the current position.

parameters.name: 'omitnan'
parameters.description: Ignore NaN values inside the window.

tools.notes: The default 'shrink' endpoint rule averages fewer points near the edges, which reduces smoothing there. The whole `mov*` family (movsum, movmax, movmin, movstd, movvar, movprod) shares this syntax.

tools.name: movmedian
tools.description: Computes a moving median over a sliding window, which removes impulsive noise and spikes far better than a moving average. Use it to despike sensor data and to estimate a robust baseline before detecting events. It shares the window, endpoint and sample-point options of the rest of the moving-statistics family.
tools.usage:
M = movmedian(A, k)
M = movmedian(A, [kb kf])
M = movmedian(___, dim)
M = movmedian(___, 'Endpoints', ep)
tools.notes: A moving median with an even window averages the two central values. It is slower than movmean because each window must be sorted.

tools.name: smoothdata
tools.description: Smooths noisy data with a chosen method: moving average, moving median, Gaussian-weighted average, Savitzky-Golay polynomial filtering, or local regression (lowess and loess). If no window is specified it chooses one heuristically from the data. Use it as the single entry point for smoothing vectors, matrices, tables and timetables.
tools.usage:
B = smoothdata(A)
B = smoothdata(A, method)
B = smoothdata(A, method, window)
B = smoothdata(___, 'SamplePoints', t)
[B, window] = smoothdata(___)

parameters.name: 'SmoothingFactor'
parameters.description: Value in [0,1] controlling the automatically chosen window.

tools.notes: The robust variants 'rlowess' and 'rloess' downweight outliers. `smoothdata2` smooths gridded 2-D data. For a linear phase filter with a known frequency response use Signal Processing Toolbox instead.

tools.name: normalize
tools.description: Rescales data by a chosen method: z-score, range scaling, norm, centring, median-IQR or scaling by a statistic. Use it to standardize features before fitting, to map data into [0,1] for display, and to make variables comparable. It works on arrays, tables and timetables, and can return the centre and scale used.
tools.usage:
N = normalize(A)
N = normalize(A, method)
N = normalize(A, method, methodtype)
N = normalize(A, dim, ___)
[N, C, S] = normalize(___)

parameters.name: methodtype
parameters.description: For 'range' a two-element interval, for 'norm' the p value, for 'center'/'scale' a statistic or value.

tools.example:
x = [2 4 6 8];
normalize(x)
normalize(x, 'range')
normalize(x, 'range', [-1 1])
[n, c, s] = normalize(x);
[c s]
normalize(x, 'center', 'median')
tools.notes: Saving the returned centre and scale lets you apply exactly the same transformation to new data, which is essential to avoid leakage in model validation.

tools.name: isoutlier
tools.description: Flags outliers using a chosen rule: scaled median absolute deviation (the default), mean plus/minus standard deviations, interquartile range, percentiles, or a moving-window version of any of these. Use it to screen measurement data before analysis and to build cleaning pipelines. Additional outputs return the lower and upper thresholds and the computed centre.
tools.usage:
TF = isoutlier(A)
TF = isoutlier(A, method)
TF = isoutlier(A, 'percentiles', threshold)
TF = isoutlier(A, movmethod, window)
[TF, L, U, C] = isoutlier(___)

parameters.name: window
parameters.description: Window length for the moving methods.

tools.notes: For data with a trend, a global method flags the extremes of the trend rather than genuine outliers; use the moving variants. `filloutliers` replaces them and `rmoutliers` deletes them.

tools.name: rmoutliers
tools.description: Removes outliers detected by the same rules as `isoutlier`, deleting entire rows for matrices and tables so that observations stay aligned. Use it as a one-line cleaning step before fitting or summarizing. The second output returns a logical vector of which entries were removed.
tools.usage:
B = rmoutliers(A)
B = rmoutliers(A, method)
B = rmoutliers(A, movmethod, window)
[B, TF] = rmoutliers(___)
B = rmoutliers(___, 'OutlierLocations', tf)

parameters.name: 'MinNumOutliers'
parameters.description: How many outliers a row must contain before it is removed.

tools.notes: For a matrix, rmoutliers removes whole rows, which can discard a lot of data when outliers are scattered. `filloutliers` is the less destructive alternative.

tools.name: fillmissing
tools.description: Replaces missing values (NaN, NaT, missing strings, undefined categoricals, empty cells) using a constant or an interpolation or fill rule. Use it to prepare data for functions that cannot handle gaps, and to reconstruct evenly sampled signals. It operates on arrays, tables and timetables and can restrict the maximum gap it will fill.
tools.usage:
F = fillmissing(A, method)
F = fillmissing(A, 'constant', v)
F = fillmissing(A, movmethod, window)
[F, TF] = fillmissing(___)
F = fillmissing(___, 'SamplePoints', t)

parameters.name: 'MaxGap'
parameters.description: Longest run of missing values that will be filled.

parameters.name: 'EndValues'
parameters.description: How to handle missing values at the ends.

tools.notes: Filling long gaps by interpolation invents data; set 'MaxGap' so that only short gaps are filled. `ismissing` finds the gaps and `rmmissing` deletes them instead.

tools.name: rmmissing
tools.description: Removes missing entries from a vector, or rows containing missing values from a matrix, table or timetable. Use it for listwise deletion before analyses that require complete cases. The optional threshold controls how many missing values a row must contain before it is dropped.
tools.usage:
R = rmmissing(A)
R = rmmissing(A, dim)
[R, TF] = rmmissing(___)
R = rmmissing(___, 'MinNumMissing', n)
R = rmmissing(___, 'DataVariables', vars)

parameters.name: dim
parameters.description: 1 to remove rows (default for tables), 2 to remove columns.

parameters.name: 'MinNumMissing'
parameters.description: Minimum number of missing values required to remove an entry.

tools.notes: Listwise deletion can bias results when data is not missing at random. Check how much you are losing with `sum(ismissing(A), 'all')` before removing.

tools.name: interp1
tools.description: Interpolates a one-dimensional function sampled at points x with values v, evaluated at query points xq. Methods range from fast piecewise linear and nearest-neighbour to shape-preserving pchip and smooth spline. Use it for resampling time series, for lookup tables and for evaluating measured curves at arbitrary points.
tools.usage:
vq = interp1(x, v, xq)
vq = interp1(x, v, xq, method)
vq = interp1(x, v, xq, method, extrapolation)
vq = interp1(v, xq)
pp = interp1(x, v, method, 'pp')

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Sample points; must be distinct and are assumed sorted for best performance.

parameters.name: v
parameters.description: Sample values; may be a matrix with one column per data set.

parameters.name: extrapolation
parameters.description: 'extrap' to extrapolate, or a scalar value for out-of-range queries.

tools.notes: Out-of-range queries return NaN unless you ask for extrapolation. 'spline' can overshoot between points while 'pchip' preserves monotonicity, which matters for physical quantities that must stay positive.

tools.name: interp2
tools.description: Interpolates a function of two variables defined on a full grid, evaluated at query points Xq, Yq. Use it for resampling images and maps, for evaluating 2-D lookup tables and for refining coarse simulation output. The grid must be plaid, as produced by `meshgrid`, and monotonic in each direction.
tools.usage:
Vq = interp2(X, Y, V, Xq, Yq)
Vq = interp2(V, Xq, Yq)
Vq = interp2(___, method)
Vq = interp2(___, method, extrapval)
Vq = interp2(V, k)

parameters.name: X, Y
parameters.description: Grid coordinate matrices in meshgrid (ndgrid-transposed) orientation.

parameters.name: extrapval
parameters.description: Value returned for queries outside the grid.

parameters.name: k
parameters.description: Refinement factor: insert 2^k-1 points between samples.

tools.notes: interp2 uses meshgrid orientation, where X varies along columns; `interpn` and `griddedInterpolant` use ndgrid orientation. Mixing the two is the most common source of transposed results.

tools.name: interp3
tools.description: Interpolates a function of three variables on a full 3-D grid at specified query points. Use it for resampling volumetric data such as MRI or CFD fields, and for evaluating 3-D lookup tables. As with interp2, the sample grid must be plaid and monotonic in each direction.
tools.usage:
Vq = interp3(X, Y, Z, V, Xq, Yq, Zq)
Vq = interp3(V, Xq, Yq, Zq)
Vq = interp3(___, method)
Vq = interp3(___, method, extrapval)
tools.notes: Memory grows as the cube of the grid resolution, so refine selectively. For large volumes build a `griddedInterpolant` once and call it repeatedly.

tools.name: interpn
tools.description: Interpolates a function of N variables on a full N-dimensional grid, generalizing interp1, interp2 and interp3. It uses ndgrid orientation, where the first dimension corresponds to the first coordinate. Use it for high-dimensional lookup tables such as engine maps and parameter sweeps.
tools.usage:
Vq = interpn(X1, ..., Xn, V, Y1, ..., Yn)
Vq = interpn(V, Y1, ..., Yn)
Vq = interpn(___, method)
Vq = interpn(___, method, extrapval)

parameters.name: X1,...,Xn
parameters.description: Grid coordinate arrays in ndgrid orientation, or coordinate vectors.

tools.notes: Passing coordinate vectors instead of full ndgrid arrays saves a lot of memory and is supported directly. Use `griddedInterpolant` when you evaluate the same table many times.

tools.name: griddata
tools.description: Interpolates scattered (non-gridded) data onto a grid or at arbitrary query points, using triangulation-based or biharmonic methods. Use it to turn irregular measurements such as survey points or sensor readings into a surface for plotting and analysis. For repeated queries on the same data, `scatteredInterpolant` is considerably faster.
tools.usage:
vq = griddata(x, y, v, xq, yq)
vq = griddata(x, y, v, xq, yq, method)
vq = griddata(x, y, z, v, xq, yq, zq)
tools.notes: Query points outside the convex hull of the data return NaN for most methods. The 'v4' method is global, smooth and slow, and ignores the convex hull restriction.

tools.name: griddedInterpolant
tools.description: Creates a reusable interpolant object for data on a full grid, so the preprocessing happens once and each evaluation is fast. Call the object like a function with query coordinates. Use it inside loops, ODE right-hand sides and optimization objectives where the same table is sampled thousands of times.
tools.usage:
F = griddedInterpolant(V)
F = griddedInterpolant(X, V)
F = griddedInterpolant(X1, ..., Xn, V)
F = griddedInterpolant(___, method, extrapmethod)
vq = F(xq)

parameters.name: X1,...,Xn
parameters.description: Grid coordinates in ndgrid orientation, or grid vectors.

parameters.name: extrapmethod
parameters.description: Extrapolation method, or 'none' to return NaN outside the grid.

tools.notes: You can change Method and ExtrapolationMethod on an existing object without rebuilding it. Building the object once is typically several times faster than repeated `interp1` calls.

tools.name: scatteredInterpolant
tools.description: Creates a reusable interpolant for scattered 2-D or 3-D data, built on a Delaunay triangulation. Call the object with query coordinates to evaluate, and change Method or ExtrapolationMethod without rebuilding. Use it instead of repeated `griddata` calls when interpolating the same scattered data many times.
tools.usage:
F = scatteredInterpolant(x, y, v)
F = scatteredInterpolant(x, y, z, v)
F = scatteredInterpolant(P, v)
F = scatteredInterpolant(___, method, extrapmethod)
vq = F(xq, yq)

parameters.name: x, y, z
parameters.description: Scattered sample coordinates as column vectors.

tools.notes: Duplicate sample points are averaged with a warning. Setting extrapolation to 'none' returns NaN outside the convex hull, which is usually safer than extrapolating scattered data.

tools.name: spline
tools.description: Performs cubic spline interpolation with not-a-knot end conditions, or returns the piecewise polynomial structure for later evaluation with `ppval`. Splines are twice continuously differentiable and therefore very smooth, but they can overshoot between data points. Supplying extra end values in v imposes clamped first-derivative end conditions.
tools.usage:
s = spline(x, y, xq)
pp = spline(x, y)

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: Sample values; two extra values clamp the end slopes.

tools.notes: Splines extrapolate beyond the data range, often wildly. For data that must stay monotone or non-negative, `pchip` or `makima` are better choices.

tools.name: pchip
tools.description: Performs shape-preserving piecewise cubic Hermite interpolation, which never overshoots and preserves the monotonicity of the data. It is only once continuously differentiable, so it is slightly less smooth than a spline. Use it for physically meaningful quantities such as concentrations, probabilities and monotone calibration curves.
tools.usage:
p = pchip(x, y, xq)
pp = pchip(x, y)
tools.notes: The spline curve dips below zero on this step-like data while pchip does not. `interp1(x,y,xq,'pchip')` is equivalent and often more readable in interpolation pipelines.

tools.name: makima
tools.description: Performs modified Akima piecewise cubic interpolation, a compromise between the smoothness of a spline and the overshoot resistance of pchip. The modification removes the spurious undulations that classic Akima interpolation produces on flat regions. Use it when spline is too wiggly but pchip looks too flat.
tools.usage:
yq = makima(x, y, xq)
pp = makima(x, y)
tools.notes: Available since R2019b and also selectable as the 'makima' method in `interp1`, `interp2`, `interpn` and `griddedInterpolant`.

tools.name: polyfit
tools.description: Fits a polynomial of degree n to data in the least-squares sense, returning the coefficients in descending power order. Optional outputs provide the error structure needed by `polyval` for prediction intervals, and centring and scaling parameters that improve conditioning for high degrees. Use it for trend lines, calibration curves and simple curve fitting without a toolbox.
tools.usage:
p = polyfit(x, y, n)
[p, S] = polyfit(x, y, n)
[p, S, mu] = polyfit(x, y, n)
tools.notes: High-degree fits on raw x are badly conditioned and MATLAB warns; use the three-output form with mu, then pass mu to `polyval`. A polynomial fit extrapolates disastrously outside the data range.

tools.name: polyval
tools.description: Evaluates a polynomial given its coefficient vector in descending powers, using Horner's method. With the error structure and centring parameters from `polyfit` it also returns standard error estimates for prediction intervals. Use it to draw fitted curves and to apply calibration polynomials to new measurements.
tools.usage:
y = polyval(p, x)
[y, delta] = polyval(p, x, S)
y = polyval(p, x, [], mu)
[y, delta] = polyval(p, x, S, mu)

parameters.name: mu
parameters.description: Centring and scaling vector [mean, std] from polyfit.

tools.example:
p = [1 -3 2];              % x^2 - 3x + 2
polyval(p, [0 1 2 3])
x = 0:0.1:4;
plot(x, polyval(p, x))
roots(p)'
tools.notes: `polyvalm` evaluates a polynomial with a matrix argument, using matrix powers instead of elementwise ones. Coefficient order is descending, the opposite of some other environments.

tools.name: roots
tools.description: Computes all roots of a polynomial given its coefficient vector, by finding the eigenvalues of the companion matrix. Roots may be complex even when the coefficients are real. Use it to solve polynomial equations, to find the poles and zeros of a transfer function, and to locate equilibrium points.
tools.usage: r = roots(p)
tools.example:
roots([1 -3 2])
roots([1 0 1])
p = poly([2 3 5]);
roots(p)'
polyval([1 -3 2], roots([1 -3 2]))
tools.notes: Root finding from coefficients is ill conditioned for high degrees and for closely spaced roots, so treat the results of degree 20 and above with suspicion. Leading zeros in p are stripped, reducing the degree.

tools.name: poly
tools.description: Builds the coefficient vector of the monic polynomial whose roots are the given values, or the characteristic polynomial of a square matrix. Use it to construct a polynomial from known zeros, to design filters by zero placement, and to obtain a characteristic polynomial for symbolic or analytic work. It is the inverse of `roots` for the root form.
tools.usage:
p = poly(r)
p = poly(A)

parameters.name: A
parameters.description: Square matrix whose characteristic polynomial is computed.

tools.example:
p = poly([1 2 3])
roots(p)'
A = [1 2; 3 4];
c = poly(A)
roots(c)'
eig(A)'
tools.notes: Computing eigenvalues via `roots(poly(A))` is much less accurate than calling `eig` directly; poly is for constructing polynomials, not for eigenvalue computation.

tools.name: polyder
tools.description: Differentiates a polynomial given by its coefficients, or differentiates the product or quotient of two polynomials when called with two inputs. Use it to find turning points by differentiating and root-finding, and for analytic derivatives of fitted curves. The result is again a coefficient vector in descending powers.
tools.usage:
k = polyder(p)
k = polyder(a, b)
[q, d] = polyder(a, b)

parameters.name: a, b
parameters.description: Two polynomials; one output gives the derivative of a*b, two outputs give the numerator and denominator of the derivative of a/b.

tools.example:
p = [1 0 -4 0];          % x^3 - 4x
dp = polyder(p)
stationary = roots(dp)'
polyder([1 1], [1 -1])
[num, den] = polyder([1 0], [1 1]);
tools.notes: For the derivative of a quotient, remember to request both outputs; with one output polyder differentiates the product instead.

tools.name: polyint
tools.description: Integrates a polynomial analytically, returning the coefficients of the antiderivative with an optional constant of integration. Use it together with `polyval` to compute exact definite integrals of polynomial fits, and in analytic area or work calculations. The result has one more coefficient than the input.
tools.usage:
q = polyint(p)
q = polyint(p, k)
tools.example:
p = [3 0 -2];             % 3x^2 - 2
q = polyint(p)
area = polyval(q, 2) - polyval(q, 0)
integral(@(x) polyval(p, x), 0, 2)
tools.notes: This is exact for polynomials, unlike `integral` or `trapz`. Combine with `polyfit` to integrate a fitted trend analytically.
